Consolidation

/kun-sol-ih-DAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Consolidation means the process of combining several separate things — often companies, offices, or duties — into one stronger, more efficient whole.

Consolidation means the process of combining several separate things into one stronger, more efficient whole. The consolidation of the town's three aging libraries into one modern branch doubled the book budget, and after a similar consolidation, the shipping company ran one big warehouse instead of five scattered ones.

Worked Example

The consolidation of the two hospitals' billing departments cut the paperwork in half and ended months of duplicated effort.

Two separate departments become one combined unit that works better and wastes less. That process of merging separate pieces into a single, more efficient whole is a consolidation.

How Consolidation Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

merger

merger: the joining of two or more organizations

unification

unification: the act of bringing parts into one

centralization

centralization: gathering control into one place

Antonyms

fragmentation

fragmentation: breaking apart into pieces

dispersal

dispersal: a scattering in different directions

How Strong Is It? — combination → consolidation → fusion

combination vs. consolidation

combination vs. consolidation: A combination is any joining of things, as casual as mixing two playlists into one.

fusion vs. consolidation

fusion vs. consolidation: A fusion goes further than a consolidation: the separate parts melt together so completely that they can no longer be told apart.

Put it together

Put it together: Consolidation is the process (-ation) of making things firm and whole (solidus) together (con-) — pressing separate, wobbly pieces into one solid block.

Root Check

Word Choice

Business / institutional

Consolidation is the go-to word when separate companies, offices, schools, or debts are combined into one stronger, more efficient unit — you'll hear it constantly in business and government news. Compare amalgamation, another word in this unit: an amalgamation blends things of different origins into a brand-new whole, while a consolidation merges similar units mainly for strength and efficiency.
